learningOutcomes: State and apply Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, including T² ∝ a³.
Apply Newton's universal law of gravitation, both to point masses and (via the shell theorem) to spherically symmetric bodies.
Compute how g varies with height above and depth below the Earth's surface, and know it is maximum at the surface.
Apply gravitational potential energy, escape speed, and the energy of an orbiting satellite.
Derive and use the orbital speed and time period of a satellite, and understand why astronauts experience weightlessness.

cheatSheet.oneLiner: Kepler's laws (observation) → Newton's law of gravitation (explanation) → shell theorem → g variation with height/depth → gravitational PE → escape speed → satellite orbits and energy.
mustKnowBullets: Kepler's 1st law (orbits): planets move in ELLIPSES with the Sun at one focus. 2nd law (areas): equal areas swept in equal times — a direct consequence of angular momentum conservation for any central force, not just gravity. 3rd law (periods): T² ∝ a³.
Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², attractive, along the line joining the masses; G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
Superposition: net gravitational force from several masses is the VECTOR sum of individual pairwise forces.

Shell theorem: a uniform spherical shell/sphere attracts an external point mass exactly as if all its mass were concentrated at the centre. Inside a uniform SHELL, the net gravitational force is ZERO everywhere.
g = GM_E/R_E² at the Earth's surface; g is MAXIMUM at the surface — it decreases both going up (g(h)=g/(1+h/R)²≈g(1−2h/R) for h≪R) and going down (g(d)=g(1−d/R)).
Gravitational PE: V(r) = −Gm₁m₂/r (taking V=0 at r=∞) — always negative for a bound configuration.
Escape speed: v_e = √(2GM_E/R_E) = √(2gR_E) ≈ 11.2 km/s from Earth's surface — independent of the projected object's mass and direction.
Orbital speed of a satellite at height h: V² = GM_E/(R_E+h); time period T = 2π(R_E+h)^(3/2)/√(GM_E) — this IS Kepler's third law applied to satellites.
Energy of a circular orbit: E = −GM_Em/2(R_E+h); K.E. = −E (positive); P.E. = 2E (negative) — total energy is exactly half the (negative) potential energy in magnitude.
Total energy negative ⟹ bound orbit (elliptical/circular); zero or positive ⟹ the object escapes to infinity.
Angular momentum and total mechanical energy are conserved for orbital motion; LINEAR momentum is NOT conserved (gravity is an external, non-uniform force on the orbiting body).
Astronauts feel weightlessness because both the astronaut and the satellite are in continuous free fall toward the Earth — NOT because gravity is 'absent' in orbit.
Gravitational shielding is impossible — unlike an electric charge inside a hollow conductor, nothing can block gravitational force from reaching a particle inside a shell from outside sources.

highlights.text: Kepler's Law of Orbits: all planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one of the two foci (not the centre) of the ellipse.
highlights.whyItMatters: Direct-recall fact; commonly tested with perihelion/aphelion (closest/farthest point) terminology.

highlights.text: Kepler's Law of Areas: the radius vector from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. This follows from conservation of angular momentum, which holds for ANY central force, not gravitation specifically.
highlights.whyItMatters: Explains WHY planets move faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion — a frequent conceptual question (Example 7.1 uses v_perihelion×r_perihelion = v_aphelion×r_aphelion).

highlights.text: Kepler's Law of Periods: T² ∝ a³, where a is the semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit (equals the radius for a circular orbit).
highlights.whyItMatters: Central numerical formula — used to compare planets/satellites/moons via ratios without needing G or M individually.

highlights.text: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation: every body in the universe attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, F = Gm₁m₂/r².
highlights.whyItMatters: The master formula of the chapter; F₁₂ = −F₂₁ by Newton's third law.

highlights.text: For a collection of point masses, the net gravitational force on any one of them is the VECTOR sum of the individual pairwise forces (principle of superposition) — each pairwise force acts independently, uninfluenced by the other bodies.
highlights.whyItMatters: Required for any multi-body gravitation problem (e.g. masses at triangle/square vertices).

highlights.text: The gravitational force between two hollow spherical shells or solid spheres of uniform density (the shell theorem): (1) OUTSIDE, the shell/sphere attracts a point mass exactly as if all its mass were concentrated at the centre; (2) INSIDE a uniform shell, the net gravitational force on a point mass is exactly ZERO everywhere.
highlights.whyItMatters: Essential for 'mass inside a tunnel through the Earth' and 'point mass inside a spherical shell' style questions; unlike electrostatic shielding, this is a genuine cancellation from symmetry, not a physical blocking mechanism.

highlights.text: Newton's law of gravitation as F=Gm₁m₂/r² applies directly only to POINT masses. For extended/finite-sized bodies, one must either use the shell-theorem shortcut (for spherically symmetric bodies) or integrate/vector-sum over all constituent point masses.
highlights.whyItMatters: Common trap — students misapply the point-mass formula directly to extended bodies without justification.

highlights.text: The value of G was first measured experimentally by Henry Cavendish (1798) using a torsion-balance apparatus; the currently accepted value is G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Since g and R_E are easily measurable, measuring G lets one deduce the mass of the Earth — popularly called 'Cavendish weighed the Earth'.
highlights.whyItMatters: Historical/conceptual fact tested directly; also the basis of 'weighing the Earth/Sun' numerical questions.

highlights.text: The acceleration due to gravity g is MAXIMUM at the Earth's surface — it decreases both as you go UP (height h) and as you go DOWN (depth d) from the surface, following different formulas in each case.
highlights.whyItMatters: A very common assertion-reason/graph-based question; students often assume g keeps increasing toward the centre, which is wrong.

highlights.text: The gravitational force is conservative, so a potential energy function exists. Gravitational PE V(r) = −Gm₁m₂/r (with the convention V=0 at r=∞) is always NEGATIVE for any finite separation — this reflects that the masses are gravitationally bound relative to being infinitely far apart.
highlights.whyItMatters: Explains why bound-orbit total energies come out negative; conceptually different from the everyday mgh formula, which is just a local approximation of this general result.

highlights.text: The familiar formula PE = mgh is only an APPROXIMATION valid close to the Earth's surface (height ≪ R_E), where gravity is nearly constant. It is a limiting case of the more general V(r) = −GMm/r, not a separate law.
highlights.whyItMatters: Frequently tested distinction — mgh cannot be used for satellite-height or escape-speed problems.

highlights.text: Escape speed is the MINIMUM initial speed needed for an object to escape a planet's gravity and just reach infinity with zero final speed: v_e = √(2GM_E/R_E) = √(2gR_E) ≈ 11.2 km/s for Earth. It does NOT depend on the mass, direction of projection, or (for a given launch point) the shape of the trajectory.
highlights.whyItMatters: One of the most frequently tested single-number facts in this chapter (11.2 km/s for Earth, ~2.3 km/s for the Moon — five times smaller, which is why the Moon has no atmosphere).

highlights.text: Earth satellites move under gravity exactly like planets around the Sun, so Kepler's laws apply equally to them. For a satellite very close to the Earth's surface (h≪R_E), the time period reduces to T₀ = 2π√(R_E/g) ≈ 85 minutes.
highlights.whyItMatters: The 85-minute 'minimum possible orbital period near Earth' figure is a frequently quoted NEET fact.

highlights.text: For a satellite in a circular orbit, total mechanical energy E = K.E. + P.E. = −GM_Em/2(R_E+h). The K.E. is positive, the P.E. is negative, and in MAGNITUDE the K.E. is exactly half the P.E. — so the total energy is negative, equal in magnitude to the K.E.
highlights.whyItMatters: Central relation for 'energy needed to boost a satellite to a higher orbit' problems (ΔE calculations).

highlights.text: Astronauts inside an orbiting satellite experience weightlessness NOT because gravity vanishes there (it is only slightly weaker than at the surface), but because both the astronaut and the satellite are continuously in free fall toward the Earth, falling together at the same rate.
highlights.whyItMatters: One of the most commonly misunderstood conceptual points, directly listed as a 'Point to Ponder' in NCERT and a frequent assertion-reason question.

highlights.text: For motion under gravity, angular momentum and total mechanical energy are conserved, but LINEAR momentum is NOT conserved (the Earth/Sun exerts an external, non-uniform force on the orbiting body throughout its path).
highlights.whyItMatters: Contrasts with the System of Particles chapter's conservation laws — a favourite conceptual trap combining two chapters.

definitions.definition: Every body in the universe attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = Gm₁m₂/r².
The universal constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², first measured by Henry Cavendish using a torsion balance.
The potential energy associated with two particles of masses m₁, m₂ separated by distance r: V(r) = −Gm₁m₂/r (taking V=0 at r=∞); always negative for a bound pair.
The gravitational potential energy per unit mass at a point due to a source mass M: U(r) = −GM/r, SI unit J kg⁻¹.
The gravitational force per unit mass at a point, a vector quantity g = (GM/r²)r̂ (directed toward the source mass), SI unit m s⁻².
The minimum speed with which an object must be projected from a planet's surface so that it just reaches infinity with zero residual speed; v_e=√(2GM/R)=√(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s for Earth.
An object revolving around the Earth under its gravitational attraction, in a circular or elliptical orbit, obeying the same Kepler's laws as planets orbiting the Sun.

The sensation of having no weight experienced by an astronaut in an orbiting satellite, arising because both the astronaut and satellite are in continuous free fall toward the Earth together — NOT because gravity is absent there.

A force on a body that is always directed along the line joining it to a fixed point (e.g. the Sun), with magnitude depending only on the distance from that point. Gravitation is one example; angular momentum is conserved for motion under ANY central force.

formulas.name: Kepler's three laws
formulas.latex: \text{(1) Elliptical orbits, Sun at a focus} \quad \text{(2)} \ \dfrac{dA}{dt}=\text{const} \quad \text{(3)} \ T^2 \propto a^3
formulas.plain: orbits are ellipses; equal areas swept in equal times; period² is proportional to semi-major-axis³

symbols.meaning: semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit

formulas.whenToUse: Comparing periods/orbital radii of different planets or satellites, or explaining why a planet speeds up near perihelion.
commonMistakes: Using the orbit's actual radius when the orbit is elliptical — must use the SEMI-MAJOR axis a, not the instantaneous distance.
Forgetting the law of areas is a general consequence of angular momentum conservation for ANY central force, not something unique to gravity.

questionPatterns.patternName: Compare orbital sizes/periods of two planets via T²∝a³
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Set up a ratio (T₁/T₂)² = (a₁/a₂)³ to avoid needing G or the central mass.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Direct ratio application of Kepler's third law.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Suppose a planet went around the Sun twice as fast as the Earth. What would be its orbital radius compared to Earth's?

questionPatterns.patternName: Relate speed and distance at perihelion vs aphelion
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Angular momentum conservation gives m r_P v_P = m r_A v_A (since r⊥v at both extreme points).
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: v_P/v_A = r_A/r_P — since r_A>r_P, the planet moves fastest at perihelion.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Relate the planet's speed and Sun-distance at perihelion to the corresponding quantities at aphelion.

formulas.audioScript: Kepler found these purely from observation, decades before Newton explained WHY they're true — the area law in particular is really just angular momentum conservation in disguise, valid for any force that always points straight at a fixed centre.

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.plain: attractive force between two point masses, proportional to the product of masses, inversely proportional to distance squared

symbols.meaning: universal gravitational constant, 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²

formulas.whenToUse: Any two-point-mass (or, via the shell theorem, spherically symmetric extended body) gravitational force calculation.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the force is ATTRACTIVE, i.e. F is along −r̂ (from m₂ toward m₁), not +r̂.
Applying this point-mass formula directly to extended/non-spherical bodies without justification.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Direct substitution once both masses and their separation are known.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the gravitational force between two 1 kg point masses separated by 1 m.

formulas.audioScript: This single inverse-square law unifies falling apples and orbiting planets — the same force law explains both, which was Newton's key insight.

formulas.name: Superposition of gravitational forces
formulas.plain: net force on one mass = vector sum of the individual forces from every other mass
formulas.whenToUse: Three or more point masses arranged in a configuration (triangle, square, line) — find the net force on one of them.
commonMistakes: Adding magnitudes directly instead of doing a proper vector sum — components along non-parallel directions must be resolved first.

questionPatterns.patternName: Net force on a mass at the centroid of a triangle of masses
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Compute each pairwise force vector, resolve into components, sum.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: By symmetry, three equal forces from three equal masses at 120° to each other sum to zero.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Three equal masses m are fixed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Find the net force on a mass 2m placed at the centroid.

formulas.audioScript: Just like electric or any other force superposition, gravity from multiple sources adds as vectors — and symmetric arrangements often let the answer come out to exactly zero without heavy calculation.

formulas.name: Shell theorem (spherical shell / solid sphere)
formulas.latex: F_{outside} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}\ (\text{as if all mass at centre}), \qquad F_{inside\ shell} = 0
formulas.plain: outside a uniform shell/sphere, gravity acts as if all mass is at the centre; inside a uniform SHELL, the net force is zero
formulas.whenToUse: Point mass inside/outside a uniform spherical shell or solid sphere — including 'tunnel through the Earth' style problems (combine with F5's g(d) formula).
commonMistakes: Applying the 'as if concentrated at centre' rule to a point INSIDE a shell — inside a shell, the force is exactly zero, not just weaker.
Forgetting a solid sphere is just a nested set of shells — a point inside a solid sphere only feels the shells INTERIOR to it (see g(d) formula).

questionPatterns.patternName: Force on a mass inside a hollow shell
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Recognize immediately that this force is zero by the shell theorem, regardless of position inside.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A hemispherical shell of uniform mass density — what is the gravitational field at the centre of the flat face?

formulas.audioScript: This is a beautiful geometric cancellation, not a physical blocking effect — every little patch of the shell pulling you one way is exactly balanced by another patch pulling you the opposite way, everywhere inside, which is also why gravitational shielding is fundamentally impossible unlike electrostatic shielding.

formulas.name: g at the surface, above, and below the Earth
formulas.latex: g=\dfrac{GM_E}{R_E^2}, \qquad g(h) = g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{R_E}\right)\ (h\ll R_E), \qquad g(d) = g\left(1-\dfrac{d}{R_E}\right)
formulas.plain: surface gravity; approximate decrease with height (small h); decrease with depth (linear, assuming uniform density)
formulas.whenToUse: Any problem about how 'weight' changes with altitude or depth (mines, tunnels, high-altitude flight, satellites close to Earth).
commonMistakes: Using the approximate g(h)≈g(1−2h/R) formula when h is comparable to R_E — the approximation requires h≪R_E; otherwise use the exact g(h)=GM/(R+h)².
Assuming g keeps increasing toward the Earth's centre — it is MAXIMUM at the surface and decreases in both directions.

questionPatterns.patternName: Weight of a body at a given height or depth
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Identify whether the point is above (use height formula) or below (use depth formula) the surface, then find the new g.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: New weight = m × g(h) or m × g(d).
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A body weighs 63 N on the Earth's surface. What is the gravitational force on it at a height equal to half the Earth's radius?

questionPatterns.patternName: Depth at which weight is halved
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Set g(d)=g/2 and solve for d/R_E.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: How much would a body weigh half way down to the Earth's centre, if it weighed 250 N on the surface (assume uniform density)?

formulas.audioScript: Remember the asymmetry — going up, g falls off roughly as an inverse-square-derived 2h/R factor, but going down through a uniformly dense Earth, g falls off perfectly linearly with depth, because only the smaller sphere interior to you contributes at all.

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy
formulas.plain: PE of two masses separated by r, taking PE to be zero at infinite separation
formulas.whenToUse: Any energy-based gravitation problem NOT restricted to near the Earth's surface — escape speed, satellite energy, multi-particle systems.
commonMistakes: Using mgh instead of −GMm/r for large height changes — mgh is only the near-surface limiting case.
Forgetting the total PE of a multi-particle system is the SUM over ALL PAIRS (superposition), not just adjacent pairs.

questionPatterns.patternName: PE and potential of a system of point masses at symmetric positions
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: For 4 equal masses at a square's corners: 4 side-pairs at distance l, 2 diagonal-pairs at distance √2 l.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the potential energy of a system of four particles of mass m placed at the vertices of a square of side l, and the gravitational potential at the centre of the square.

formulas.audioScript: Gravitational PE is always negative in this convention, because you'd have to do positive work to pull the masses apart to infinity — a smaller (more negative) PE means a more tightly bound system.

formulas.name: Escape speed
formulas.plain: minimum launch speed so total mechanical energy is exactly zero, allowing the object to just reach infinity
formulas.whenToUse: Any 'will this object escape the planet/moon's gravity' problem.
commonMistakes: Thinking escape speed depends on launch angle or the mass of the projected object — it depends ONLY on the planet's M and R (or equivalently g and R).
Forgetting v_e is derived by setting TOTAL energy (KE+PE) to exactly zero, the boundary between escaping and remaining bound.

questionPatterns.patternName: Direct escape speed calculation / comparison between bodies
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Apply v_e=√(2gR) using the given body's own g and R.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Direct substitution; Moon's v_e is about 5× smaller than Earth's, which is why the Moon has no atmosphere.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: The escape speed of a projectile from Earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. If a body is projected with thrice this speed, find its speed far away from Earth.

formulas.audioScript: Escape speed is exactly the launch speed at which your total mechanical energy is zero — any less and you're gravitationally bound and fall back; any more and you retain leftover kinetic energy even at infinity.

formulas.name: Orbital speed and period of a satellite
formulas.plain: speed and period of a circular orbit at height h; near-surface period is about 85 minutes
formulas.whenToUse: Any circular satellite-orbit problem — finding speed, period, or comparing satellites at different altitudes.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add the Earth's radius R_E to the height h to get the actual orbital radius from the Earth's centre.
Confusing this satellite T² = k(R_E+h)³ relation with Kepler's third law about the Sun — they're the same LAW, applied to a different central body.

questionPatterns.patternName: Find orbital speed/period at a given height
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Substitute h into V²=GM_E/(R_E+h) directly, or use ratios with the near-surface T₀ if only relative comparisons are needed.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Direct substitution; equate centripetal force requirement to gravitational force to derive V² in the first place.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the orbital period of a satellite orbiting very close to the Earth's surface, given g=9.8 m/s² and R_E=6400 km.

formulas.audioScript: This formula comes from simply setting the required centripetal force equal to the gravitational force providing it — and once you see that, it's really Kepler's third law in a new outfit, just with the Earth as the central body instead of the Sun.

formulas.name: Energy of an orbiting satellite
formulas.plain: kinetic energy is positive and half the magnitude of the (negative) potential energy; total energy is negative
formulas.whenToUse: Any 'energy needed to move a satellite to a different orbit' or 'total energy of an orbiting body' problem.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the total energy is NEGATIVE for any bound circular/elliptical orbit — zero or positive total energy means the object is NOT bound (it escapes).
Sign errors: K is positive, V is negative, and |K| = |V|/2 exactly.

questionPatterns.patternName: Energy required to raise a satellite's orbit
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Compute total energy at both orbits, take the difference.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A 400 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 2R_E about the Earth. How much energy is required to transfer it to a circular orbit of radius 4R_E?

formulas.audioScript: The neat 1:2 ratio between kinetic and potential energy magnitudes is a signature of any inverse-square-law circular orbit — and it's why moving a satellite to a HIGHER orbit actually requires energy even though it ends up moving SLOWER there, since the potential energy gain outweighs the kinetic energy loss.

stages.question: State Kepler's Law of Periods.
stages.interpretation: Direct recall of the third law.
solutionSteps: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit

flashcards.audioScript: This is the law that let Newton connect the dots — apply the inverse-square force law to a circular orbit and this exact relationship falls straight out.

stages.question: What is the gravitational force on a point mass placed inside a uniform hollow spherical shell?
stages.interpretation: Direct application of the shell theorem's second result.
solutionSteps: By symmetry, contributions from all regions of the shell cancel exactly
This holds no matter where inside the shell the point mass is located

flashcards.audioScript: It doesn't matter if you're dead centre or just barely inside the shell wall — the pull is exactly zero at every interior point, a genuinely exact result, not an approximation.

stages.question: The escape speed from Earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. A body is projected with thrice this speed. Find its speed far from Earth.
stages.interpretation: Use energy conservation: leftover KE at infinity = initial KE − energy needed to just escape.

flashcards.audioScript: Since escape speed is defined by exactly using up all the kinetic energy needed to reach infinity, any speed beyond that leaves a well-defined leftover speed — subtract the energies, not the speeds directly.

stages.question: A body weighs 63 N on Earth's surface. Find the gravitational force on it at a height equal to half the Earth's radius.
stages.interpretation: Use the exact inverse-square g(h) formula since h=R/2 is NOT small compared to R.

flashcards.audioScript: With h comparable to R, you must use the exact inverse-square formula rather than the small-h linear approximation — here that's a factor of (1/1.5)² on the original weight.

stages.question: How much would a body weigh half way down to the Earth's centre, if it weighed 250 N on the surface (assume uniform density)?
stages.interpretation: Depth formula is exactly linear in d/R (unlike the height case).

flashcards.audioScript: Going down through a uniformly dense planet is simpler than going up — the weight just scales linearly, straight to zero at the very centre.

stages.question: Find the orbital period of a satellite orbiting very close to Earth's surface. (g=9.8 m/s², R_E=6400 km)
stages.interpretation: Direct substitution into the near-surface satellite period formula.

flashcards.audioScript: This 85-minute figure is essentially the shortest possible orbital period around Earth — any real satellite orbiting higher up takes longer than this.

stages.question: Three equal masses m are fixed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1 m. Find the net gravitational force on a mass 2m placed at the centroid.
stages.interpretation: By the 3-fold rotational symmetry of the configuration, the three equal-magnitude force vectors (each at 120° to the next) must sum to exactly zero.
stages.formula: Vector superposition of three equal forces at 120° to each other
solutionSteps: Each force has the same magnitude Gm(2m)/1² by symmetry (equal distances to centroid)
Three equal vectors spaced 120° apart always sum to zero
stages.answer: Net force = 0 (by symmetry — confirmed by direct vector addition in NCERT Example 7.2)

flashcards.audioScript: Whenever you see a symmetric arrangement like this, check for a zero-by-symmetry shortcut before grinding through the full vector algebra — three equal vectors at 120° always cancel perfectly.

stages.question: A 400 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 2R_E. How much energy is required to transfer it to a circular orbit of radius 4R_E?
stages.interpretation: Compute total orbital energy at both radii using E=−GM_Em/2r, take the difference.
stages.formula: ΔE = E_final − E_initial = GM_Em/8R_E (using r=4R_E and r=2R_E)
stages.answer: ≈ 3.13 × 10⁹ J (NCERT Example 7.8 — also note ΔK=−ΔE and ΔV=2ΔE)

flashcards.audioScript: Counterintuitively, moving to a HIGHER, slower orbit still costs energy overall — the satellite loses kinetic energy but gains even more potential energy, and the net total energy always increases (becomes less negative) as you climb.

conceptWarmup: Why does a planet move fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion?
Why is gravitational shielding (unlike electrostatic shielding) fundamentally impossible?
Why do astronauts in orbit experience weightlessness even though gravity there is only slightly weaker than at Earth's surface?

basic.question: Find the gravitational force between two 1 kg point masses separated by 1 m.
basic.interpretation: Direct substitution into Newton's law of gravitation.
basic.audioScript: This tiny number is exactly why we never notice gravity between everyday objects — it only becomes significant with astronomically large masses.

basic.question: Io, a moon of Jupiter, has an orbital period of 1.769 days and orbital radius 4.22×10⁸ m. Show the mass of Jupiter is about one-thousandth that of the Sun. (Earth's orbital radius=1.5×10¹¹ m, period=365.25 days)
basic.interpretation: Apply Kepler's third law twice — once for Io around Jupiter, once for Earth around the Sun — then take the ratio.
steps: Substituting the given numbers yields a ratio close to 1/1000
basic.audioScript: You don't need G at all here — take the ratio of Kepler's third law applied to each system, and the constants cancel out, leaving just a comparison of the given radii and periods.

basic.question: The escape speed of a projectile on the Moon's surface is about 2.3 km/s, roughly five times smaller than Earth's. Why does the Moon have essentially no atmosphere while Earth does?
basic.interpretation: Conceptual application of escape speed vs the thermal speeds of gas molecules.
steps: Gas molecule thermal speeds at a given temperature don't depend on which planet/moon they're on
If a significant fraction of molecules exceed the LOCAL escape speed, the atmosphere leaks away over time
The Moon's much lower escape speed means far more molecules routinely exceed it
basic.answer: The Moon's escape speed (2.3 km/s) is low enough that ordinary gas molecule speeds regularly exceed it, so any atmosphere the Moon once had has long since escaped into space.
basic.audioScript: Escape speed sets the bar a gas molecule must clear to permanently leave — and the Moon's bar is set so low that its atmosphere drained away over geological time.

intermediate.question: A rocket is fired vertically with a speed of 5 km/s from Earth's surface. How far from Earth does the rocket go before returning? (M_E=6.0×10²⁴ kg, R_E=6.4×10⁶ m, G=6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
intermediate.interpretation: Energy conservation between the launch point and the highest point (where speed=0), using the exact −GMm/r potential, not mgh.
steps: Solve for r_max using the given numbers
intermediate.answer: r_max ≈ 1.28×10⁷ m from Earth's centre, i.e. about 6.4×10⁶ m (one Earth radius) above the surface
intermediate.audioScript: Because 5 km/s is a significant fraction of the 11.2 km/s escape speed, you cannot use mgh here — the exact −GMm/r potential energy is essential once the height becomes comparable to the Earth's own radius.

intermediate.question: A satellite orbits the Earth at height 400 km above the surface. How much energy must be expended to rocket it out of Earth's gravitational influence entirely? (m=200 kg, M_E=6.0×10²⁴ kg, R_E=6.4×10⁶ m, G=6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
intermediate.interpretation: The energy needed to send it to infinity (E=0) equals minus its current (negative) total orbital energy.
intermediate.answer: ≈ 5.9 × 10⁹ J (matches NCERT's stated order of magnitude for this exercise)
intermediate.audioScript: Since the satellite's total energy is already negative (bound), you simply need to supply exactly that much positive energy to bring its total energy up to zero — the threshold for escaping entirely.

intermediate.question: Two heavy spheres, each of mass 100 kg and radius 0.10 m, are placed 1.0 m apart on a table. What is the gravitational force and potential at the midpoint of the line joining their centres?
intermediate.interpretation: By symmetry the two equal, opposite forces cancel to zero at the midpoint, but the (scalar) potentials from both spheres ADD.
steps: Force: equal magnitudes G(100)(m_test)/(0.5)² from each side, in OPPOSITE directions ⟹ net force = 0
intermediate.answer: Net force = 0; potential ≈ −2.67×10⁻⁸ J/kg. The midpoint is an equilibrium, but it is UNSTABLE (a small displacement toward either sphere increases that sphere's pull, moving the object further off-centre).
intermediate.audioScript: Force is a vector so opposing contributions can cancel to zero, but potential is a scalar so it never cancels — it just adds up, always making this midpoint a point of minimum (most negative) potential along the line, yet an unstable equilibrium in 3D.

advanced.question: Two uniform solid spheres of equal radii R, masses M and 4M, have centres 6R apart and are held fixed. A projectile of mass m is fired from the surface of the M-sphere directly toward the 4M-sphere. Find the minimum speed needed for the projectile to just reach the neutral point (where the two gravitational pulls cancel).
advanced.interpretation: First locate the neutral point using force balance, then apply energy conservation between launch and the neutral point (where speed→0).
steps: Neutral point at distance r from M: GMm/r² = G(4M)m/(6R−r)² ⟹ r=2R (from NCERT Example 7.4)
Energy conservation: ½mv² − GMm/R − 4GMm/5R = −GMm/2R − GMm/R (energies at launch and at N)
advanced.audioScript: This is a genuinely two-source problem — first find where the two pulls exactly cancel using a simple algebraic force balance, then treat that neutral point as your energy-conservation target, since the projectile only needs to just barely crawl to it before the stronger sphere's pull takes over.

advanced.question: Two stars, each of one solar mass (2×10³⁰ kg), approach each other for a head-on collision. When they are at a distance 10⁹ km apart, their speeds are negligible. What is their speed when they collide? (radius of each star = 10⁴ km)
advanced.interpretation: Use energy conservation for the two-body system, converting lost gravitational PE into kinetic energy of both stars, then use momentum conservation (equal masses ⟹ equal speeds) to split the KE.
steps: Total PE lost = Gm²[1/r_final − 1/r_initial], where r_final=2×10⁴ km (surfaces touching) and r_initial=10⁹ km
By symmetry (equal masses, starting at rest, momentum conserved), both stars have equal and opposite velocities at every instant
½(2m)v² = Gm²(1/r_final − 1/r_initial) [total KE split equally by symmetry], solve for v
advanced.answer: v ≈ 1.63×10⁶ m/s per star (order-of-magnitude NCERT answer for this exercise)
advanced.audioScript: The trick here is recognising that equal masses starting from rest must always move with equal and opposite speeds by momentum conservation — that symmetry is what lets you split the total kinetic energy released cleanly in half.

advanced.question: Weighing the Earth: given g=9.81 m/s², R_E=6.37×10⁶ m, the Earth-Moon distance R=3.84×10⁸ m and the Moon's orbital period 27.3 days, find the mass of the Earth in TWO different ways and compare.
advanced.interpretation: Method 1 uses g=GM/R_E² directly; Method 2 treats the Moon as a satellite and uses Kepler's third law.
steps: Method 2: T²=4π²R³/(GM_E) ⟹ M_E=4π²R³/(GT²), with T=27.3×24×3600 s
advanced.answer: Both methods agree to within about 1% (NCERT Example 7.6) — cross-validating G, g, and the Moon's orbital data.
advanced.audioScript: Two completely independent routes — one using surface gravity, one using the Moon's orbit as a giant natural satellite experiment — arrive at essentially the same mass for the Earth, which is a nice built-in consistency check on the whole theory.

selfCheck.q: State Kepler's Law of Areas and explain what conservation law it follows from.
selfCheck.a: The radius vector from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times — this follows from conservation of angular momentum, valid for any central force, not just gravitation.

selfCheck.q: What are the two results of the shell theorem?
selfCheck.a: Outside a uniform shell/sphere, gravity acts as if all the mass were concentrated at the centre; inside a uniform shell, the net gravitational force is exactly zero everywhere.

selfCheck.q: Why is g maximum at the Earth's surface rather than at the centre?
selfCheck.a: Going up, g falls off by the inverse-square law; going down, only the smaller interior sphere of mass contributes (shell theorem), so g also falls off — making the surface the maximum.

selfCheck.q: What determines a planet's escape speed, and what does NOT affect it?
selfCheck.a: Escape speed depends only on the planet's mass and radius (v_e=√(2GM/R)); it does NOT depend on the projected object's own mass or the direction of projection.

selfCheck.q: Why do astronauts in an orbiting satellite feel weightless?
selfCheck.a: Because both the astronaut and the satellite are in continuous free fall toward the Earth together — not because gravity is absent in orbit.
